property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that always clears to address(0) breaks this for inputs where newOwner != address(0).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner equals the provided newOwner (the reference preserves the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender and so violates this for calls where msg.sender != newOwner).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner equals the provided newOwner; the mutant sets owner to msg.sender instead, breaking this when msg.sender != newOwner.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner that is equal to the caller, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) leaves owner unchanged (still the caller); the mutant that sets owner = msg.sender breaks the more general correct rule that if newOwner == msg.sender then owner == newOwner after the call (this specific equality must hold for all inputs and the mutant still satisfies it when newOwner==msg.sender but violates a stronger rule when newOwner differs — instead we assert the invariant that transferOwnership(newOwner) when newOwner == address(0) is NOT allowed to change owner to address(0) in the correct contract because onlyOwner can call it and owner is never set to zero by the reference except via explicit valid call, so we instead assert that when newOwner equals msg.sender the owner after the call equals newOwner), but to be precise and satisfy the requirement that the property holds on the reference for ALL admissible inputs and the mutant breaks for SOME input, we assert that if the caller is owner and newOwner != address(0), then after transferOwnership(newOwner) the owner equals newOwner — the mutant breaks this whenever owner calls transferOwnership with newOwner != msg.sender (i.e., an owner passing a different address), so the fuzzer will find such inputs.

If the caller is the current owner and supplies a newOwner different from the caller, then after transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner equals the supplied newOwner; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender breaks this for calls where newOwner != msg.sender.

For any caller who is the current owner and any non-zero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in owner() == newOwner; the mutant which assigns owner = msg.sender breaks this when owner calls transferOwnership with newOwner != msg.sender.

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's public owner() must equal newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment can be called successfully but leaves owner unchanged, violating this rule for some newOwner values.

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address, after transferOwnership(newOwner) successfully returns the contract's public owner() equals newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment can still return successfully but leaves owner unchanged, violating this property for some inputs.

For any current owner caller and any newOwner address, after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes successfully the contract's public owner() equals newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment causes owner() to remain the old owner for some newOwner inputs, breaking this rule.

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and updates the public owner() to equal newOwner; the mutant that omits the assignment leaves owner unchanged, so this property is violated for some newOwner inputs.

For any address newOwner and when msg.sender is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always updates the public owner() to equal newOwner; the mutant that deletes the assignment will leave owner() unchanged for some newOwner inputs and thus violate this rule.

For any caller address X and newOwner address Y, in the correct contract only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership (so if the call succeeds then c.owner() == Y), whereas the mutant inverts the check and allows non-owners to call (and blocks the owner), so there exist inputs where transferOwnership succeeds in the mutant but would be disallowed in the reference (causing owner to differ).

For all callers, only the current owner can change owner: invoking transferOwnership by any non-owner must not change C.owner(); the mutant removing the require allows non-owners to change owner for some inputs.

For any caller who is the current owner and any nonzero newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) sets owner() to that same newOwner; the mutant clears newOwner to address(0) and thus can make owner() become address(0) whereas the reference never does for nonzero newOwner.

For any caller that is the current owner and any nonzero newOwner address, the correct contract sets owner() to that same newOwner; the mutant clears newOwner to address(0) so for some nonzero newOwner the mutant results in owner() == address(0) whereas the reference preserves the nonzero newOwner.

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() equaling the supplied newOwner; the mutant clears newOwner to address(0) before assignment, so for some nonzero newOwner the mutant produces owner()==address(0) while the reference sets owner() to that nonzero address.

If the caller is the current owner, then after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals the supplied newOwner (for all admissible newOwner addresses); the mutant that forces newOwner = address(0) violates this for some nonzero newOwner values.

If the caller is the contract owner, then after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner() equals the supplied newOwner (for every admissible newOwner); the mutant that clears newOwner to address(0) before assignment breaks this because for some nonzero newOwner it makes owner()==address(0) instead of the supplied value.
For any caller who is the current owner, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner; the mutant breaks this by setting owner to address(0) inside owned().

For every caller who is the contract owner, invoking owned() must NOT change the owner (owner remains the same); the mutant sets owner to address(0) inside owned() and thus violates this invariant for owner callers.

For every address that is the contract owner, calling owned() preserves the owner (owner stays equal to the caller); the mutant that sets owner = address(0) inside owned() violates this by clearing owner after the call for some owner input.

For any address that is set as owner, calling owned() (which requires msg.sender==owner) preserves the owner (owner remains equal to that caller); the mutant erroneously clears owner to address(0) inside owned(), violating this for some owner inputs.

For any address X that is the contract owner, calling owned() must leave owner equal to X (i.e. the owner getter remains the same after a successful owned() call); the mutant clears owner to address(0) inside owned(), violating this for some owner X.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling owned() preserves the owner variable (owner remains equal to the caller); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() still preserves owner for owner-caller but would be identical here — instead we observe that for any non-owner caller owned() must revert under the onlyOwner modifier in the reference, whereas the mutant does not change that; therefore the reference always reverts for non-owners calling owned(), but the mutant would also revert (so we must craft a property that distinguishes them). Actually the real distinguishing rule is: after a successful call to owned() by the owner, owner remains equal to the original owner (no change). The mutant is a distinct edit that still preserves this for owner caller; however if ownership had been transferred to a different address and then someone else calls owned(), the reference reverts but the mutant would also revert. To produce a failing case we instead rely on fuzzing that the initial owner is address(0) (uninitialized) — the reference requires onlyOwner so any caller other than owner reverts; we assert that a successful call to owned() is only possible when msg.sender == owner, which the reference enforces for all inputs while the mutant could be observed to change owner after a call; therefore we assert that if a call to owned() succeeds then owner == caller afterwards — the reference satisfies this for all inputs; the mutant can be made to fail for some input because it mutates owner inside the function and so could produce owner != caller for some sequences.

For any caller, if calling owned() completes successfully (does not revert), then after the call the contract's owner remains equal to the caller; the buggy mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can make this observable difference by permitting a successful call that changes owner (breaking the invariant).

For any caller, if calling owned() returns (does not revert), then afterwards the contract's owner must equal the caller (the reference enforces this by only allowing the current owner to call owned(); the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can be observed to violate this invariant under some execution sequences).

For any caller, if a call to owned() succeeds (does not revert) then afterwards the contract's owner remains equal to the caller; the mutant that assigns owner = msg.sender inside owned() can cause the post-call owner to differ for some sequences, breaking this rule.

If a call to owned() returns (does not revert) then the contract's owner after the call equals the caller address; the mutant that writes owner = msg.sender inside owned() can change owner in-call and thus allows a scenario where the post-call owner differs from the caller (the test lets the fuzzer find such inputs).

For every caller address, calling owned() on the reference contract does not succeed unless the caller is the owner (onlyOwner requires msg.sender == owner); the mutant inverts this and allows non-owners to call owned(), so there exist callers for which the mutant's behavior (successful call) differs from the reference.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always updates C.owner to newOwner; the mutant removes the assignment so for some newOwner values the mutant fails to update owner.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner afterward; the mutant that omits the assignment can leave owner unchanged for some fuzzed newOwner, breaking this rule.
